clinicalPearls: Classic biphasic course: severe hypotonia and poor feeding in infancy followed by insatiable appetite and progressive obesity in early childhood
Neonates often show a weak cry, poor suck requiring assisted feeding, and delayed milestones
Later features include short stature, small hands and feet, hypogonadism, and characteristic facial features such as a narrow bifrontal diameter and almond-shaped eyes
Hyperphagia with food-seeking behaviour can lead to life-threatening obesity if intake is not strictly controlled
Behavioural and cognitive issues include mild to moderate intellectual disability, temper outbursts, skin-picking, and obsessive traits
Caused by loss of paternally expressed genes on chromosome 15q11-q13, most often paternal deletion, less often maternal uniparental disomy
The reciprocal parental defect at the same locus produces Angelman syndrome, illustrating genomic imprinting
Growth hormone therapy improves body composition, growth, and muscle tone under specialist supervision
reference.pathophysiology: Prader-Willi syndrome arises from loss of function of paternally expressed, imprinted genes in the 15q11-q13 region. Because maternal copies of these genes are normally silenced by imprinting, absence of the paternal contribution leaves the region functionally inactive. This most commonly results from a de novo paternal deletion, and less commonly from maternal uniparental disomy (two maternal copies and no paternal copy) or an imprinting defect. Hypothalamic dysfunction is central to the phenotype, driving the abnormal satiety regulation and hyperphagia, growth hormone deficiency, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, and temperature and sleep disturbances.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of neonatal hypotonia such as spinal muscular atrophy and congenital myopathies
Bardet-Biedl syndrome and other obesity syndromes
additionalInvestigations: DNA methylation analysis of the 15q11-q13 region as the primary diagnostic test
Follow-up testing to define the mechanism (deletion, uniparental disomy, or imprinting defect) for counselling
Growth, endocrine, and pubertal assessment including growth hormone and thyroid evaluation
Sleep study to assess for obstructive and central sleep apnoea
Monitoring for obesity-related complications including glucose intolerance
redFlags: Uncontrolled hyperphagia leading to morbid obesity and its cardiorespiratory and metabolic complications
Increased risk of sudden death related to obesity and sleep-disordered breathing
Gastric distension or rupture from binge eating, which may present without typical pain
Scoliosis and respiratory compromise requiring surveillance
reference.prognosis: With rigorous dietary control, a structured food-secure environment, and growth hormone therapy, individuals can achieve improved health and function; without weight control, morbid obesity substantially shortens life expectancy.
pitfalls: Attributing neonatal hypotonia to birth injury or a primary neuromuscular disorder and delaying methylation testing
Underestimating the intensity of environmental food control required
Missing hypogonadism and osteoporosis risk in adolescents and adults
Overlooking central adrenal insufficiency and sleep apnoea
management: Recombinant growth hormone therapy to improve linear growth, body composition, muscle tone and development
Strict lifelong caloric restriction within a structured, food-secure environment to prevent life-threatening obesity from hyperphagia
Sex-hormone replacement for hypogonadotropic hypogonadism to support pubertal development and bone health
Assess for obstructive and central sleep apnoea with a sleep study before and during growth hormone therapy, treating as required
Early physiotherapy, occupational and speech therapy for infantile hypotonia and developmental delay, with assisted feeding when suck is poor
Behavioural and psychological support for temper outbursts, skin-picking and obsessive traits
Surveillance for obesity-related complications including glucose intolerance and type 2 diabetes
Genetic counselling with mechanism-specific recurrence-risk advice for deletion, maternal uniparental disomy or imprinting defect
